484.title: Daughters of Jerusalem (Luke 23:27–31)
484.hook: on the road he turns to the weeping women
484.howItsDone: Many Catholics pray the Stations of the Cross on the Fridays of Lent, walking from one image to the next around the church; the eighth station is Jesus meeting the women of Jerusalem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Herod's mockery: a ruler who wanted a show and got silence. Your line was silence before Herod. Now a new week, on the road to the cross.

On the wall of a parish church hangs the eighth of the traditional Stations of the Cross: Jesus meets the women of Jerusalem. Often it's a carved panel, a bent figure with the cross and a few women with their hands to their faces. The scene comes from Luke alone. The sentence has been passed. Jesus is being led away, and the soldiers have seized a man named Simon of Cyrene, coming in from the country, to carry the cross behind him. A great crowd follows, and among them women who bewail and lament him. He stops, turns, and speaks to them.
screen: `THE EIGHTH STATION.` → `SIMON CARRIES THE CROSS.` → `WOMEN MOURNING ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Daughters of Jerusalem, weep not over me; but weep for yourselves, and for your children." It's startling from a man on his way to be crucified. Someone else carries his cross, and his attention goes outward, to the people beside the road and to what is coming for their city. Luke has prepared us: a few chapters back, Jesus wept over Jerusalem as he rode toward it. Now he turns the women's tears the same way. He speaks of days when people will call the childless blessed, and ask the mountains to fall on them. Then a proverb readers still turn over: "For if in the green wood they do these things, what shall be done in the dry?" Green wood doesn't catch easily; dry wood does. One common reading: if they do this to the innocent one, what will happen when the times get truly dry and hard? Some readers connect the warning with the later Roman destruction of Jerusalem. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't brush the women off or call their tears wrong. He takes them seriously enough to answer, and points their grief at the people they love. The scene became a station on the Way of the Cross, and it shows something hard to fake: in the middle of his own suffering, he still sees the people in front of him.
screen: `WEEP NOT OVER ME.` · `WEEP FOR YOUR CHILDREN.` · `GREEN WOOD AND DRY.` · `HE STILL SEES THEM.`

segments.voice: Let whatever is heavy for you right now be there; don't push it away. Then, gently, look past it to one face near you this week, a tired coworker, a quiet kid, a parent who changed the subject, and hold it next to your own trouble, not instead of it. If you pray, pray for them by name; if you don't, just keep them in mind a while.
Green wood. Jesus' proverb to the weeping women on the road to his death: if they do this in the green wood, what in the dry? Today's word.
Your line: weep for yourselves. Even on that road, he turned toward them. Rest well.

485.title: Father, forgive them (Luke 23:34)
485.hook: for they know not what they do
485.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 23:34 in the Passion on Palm Sunday in the year of Luke, and some parishes keep a Good Friday devotion on the Seven Last Words, of which this is counted the first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, green wood: on the road, he turned and answered the women's tears. Your line was weep for yourselves.

The place is called Calvary, the skull. Two criminals are led out with him, one on his right and one on his left. Luke tells it almost without detail: they crucified him there. No nails described, no long account of pain. Soon the soldiers will be casting lots for his clothes. And into that ordinary cruelty, the first thing Luke has Jesus say from the cross is not a cry of pain and not a curse. It's a prayer, and it begins with today's word.
screen: `A PLACE CALLED CALVARY.` → `TWO CRIMINALS, ONE EACH SIDE.` → `THE FIRST WORD FROM THE CROSS.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus said: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Start with Father. Jesus has called God Father all through Luke: at twelve in the temple, I must be about my Father's business; in the garden, Father, if thou wilt. Nailed to wood, he still prays the same way. The relationship holds, even here. Then, forgive them. Who is them? Luke doesn't say. The soldiers, surely, who are doing the nailing. Some readers widen it to everyone who brought him here. Then the reason: they know not what they do. Not that it's fine, or that it doesn't matter. Only that they don't fully see what they're doing. Catholic devotion counts this as the first of the Seven Last Words, sayings of Jesus from the cross gathered from all four Gospels, and some parishes keep a Good Friday devotion that preaches on them one by one. And Luke shows the prayer didn't end at the cross. In his second book, Acts, the deacon Stephen, dying under stones, prays nearly the same prayer for the people throwing them. It's the hardest forgiveness there is, given while the hurt is still happening.
screen: `FATHER, EVEN HERE.` · `FORGIVE THEM: WHO IS THEM?` · `THE FIRST OF SEVEN LAST WORDS.` · `STEPHEN PRAYS IT TOO.` · then, large: `FOR THEY KNOW NOT WHAT THEY DO.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who hurt you without understanding it, a parent who said the wrong thing, a friend who never noticed what they missed, a careless stranger, and hold them in mind with the words they know not. It doesn't excuse what happened, and it doesn't mean you have to go back. If you pray, use the prayer from the cross for them; if not, just loosen your grip a little.

486.title: The centurion glorifies God (Luke 23:44–49)
486.hook: Indeed this was a just man, and the crowds go home beating their breasts
486.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of the death in the Palm Sunday Passion in the year of Luke, and pray "into thy hands" from Psalm 31 each night at Compline; at Mass they strike the breast during the Confiteor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Father: the first word from the cross, Father, forgive them. Your line was they know not.

At every Mass, near the start, Catholics say the Confiteor, the I confess. At the words through my fault, the missal has the people strike their breast: a small, old gesture, a closed hand to the chest. Where does it come from? One place it shows up is today's reading. About the sixth hour, around noon, on the day of the crucifixion, darkness comes over the whole earth until the ninth hour. The veil of the temple is torn down the middle. Jesus cries out with a loud voice, and dies. Then Luke turns the camera away from the cross, to the people standing in front of it.
screen: `A HAND TO THE CHEST AT MASS.` → `DARKNESS AT THE SIXTH HOUR.` → `THE CAMERA TURNS TO THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: Luke's Jesus dies with a psalm on his lips: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." It's from Psalm thirty, thirty-one in other Bibles, a prayer of trust the Church prays at Compline, its prayer before sleep. Then Luke shows three reactions. First, the centurion, the Roman officer in charge, who watched it all up close: "Now the centurion, seeing what was done, glorified God, saying: Indeed this was a just man." Matthew and Mark have him say Son of God. Luke has a just man, innocent, righteous, and frames it as praise: the first reaction Luke reports after the death is a Roman officer glorifying God. Second, the crowds. They came to see a spectacle, and they go home striking their breasts. No speech, just a gesture of grief and something like guilt. Third, his friends. All his acquaintances, and the women who had followed him from Galilee, stood afar off, watching. They can't do anything. They stay. Some see clearly and say so. Some feel it in the chest and go home changed. Some refuse to look away. Catholic devotion names that last kind from the old hymn Stabat Mater, the mother standing. Luke doesn't name Mary here; John does. But the women who watch him die are the women who will go to the tomb.
screen: `INTO THY HANDS.` · `A SOLDIER SAYS: A JUST MAN.` · `THE CROWD STRIKES THEIR BREASTS.` · `THE WOMEN STAND AFAR OFF.`

segments.voice: If there's a crucifix near you, look at it; if not, picture one, or simply that hill in the afternoon dark. Don't try to feel anything in particular; just stay, the way the women stayed, afar off and watching, and come back to the picture when your mind wanders. If you pray, say his last line from the psalm, into thy hands; if you don't, just keep your attention there.

487.title: Idle tales (Luke 23:55–24:12)
487.hook: the women tell the apostles, and the words seem like idle tales
487.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's account of the empty tomb at the Easter Vigil in the year of Luke, the night the Alleluia returns after Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dikaios: at the cross a centurion said, indeed this was a just man. Your line was a just man.

Friday evening. The women from Galilee follow the body to the tomb and watch exactly where it's laid. They go home and prepare spices and ointments, and on the Sabbath, Luke says, they rest, according to the commandment. Saturday is long and silent. Very early on Sunday, in the half dark, they walk back carrying the spices, to do the last thing love can do for the dead. The stone is rolled back. The body is gone. And two men in shining clothes are standing there. Today, the first people to hear the news, and the first not to be believed.
screen: `THEY WATCH WHERE HE IS LAID.` → `A SILENT SABBATH.` → `SPICES AT DAWN, AN EMPTY TOMB.`

segments.voice: The two men ask the question that turns the whole Gospel: "Why seek you the living with the dead? He is not here, but is risen." Remember what he told you in Galilee. And they remembered his words. So the women go back and tell the eleven and all the rest. Luke names them: Mary Magdalen, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and other women with them. Here's how the news lands: "And these words seemed to them as idle tales; and they did not believe them." The Greek word is leros, and it's blunt: nonsense, silly talk, a word a medical writer of the time might use for the babbling of someone in a fever. The apostles, chosen and trained for three years, hear the first announcement of the resurrection and call it nonsense. Luke doesn't hide it. He could have. Peter does get up and run to the tomb. He stoops down, sees the linen cloths lying by themselves, and goes home wondering. Not believing yet. Wondering. The women had no body and no proof: an empty space, two strangers, and a memory. Earlier in Luke, when Jesus told the twelve what would happen in Jerusalem, they understood none of it. Now the women carry those same words back to them. The first people sent to say he is risen are the ones who came at dawn to anoint a corpse.
screen: `WHY SEEK THE LIVING WITH THE DEAD?` · `THE WOMEN REMEMBER, AND TELL.` · `LEROS: IT SOUNDED LIKE NONSENSE.` · `PETER RUNS, AND WONDERS.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who told you something good lately and got a shrug back: a kid's story about their day, a friend saying things are finally getting better, a coworker excited about an idea you assumed wouldn't work. Picture their face, hear it again, and this time let it be true and be glad with them. If you pray, thank God for their news.
Idle tales. What the apostles called the women's report of the empty tomb. In Greek, leros: nonsense. They were wrong. Today's word.
Your line: not idle tales. The first news of the empty tomb came from the women. See you tomorrow.

488.title: Emmaus, slowly (Luke 24:13–35)
488.hook: stay with us, because it is towards evening
488.howItsDone: Catholics hear the Emmaus story in Easter week and on the Third Sunday of Easter in one year of the cycle, and Catholic teaching points to it as the pattern of the Mass: the Liturgy of the Word, then the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, idle tales: the women's news from the empty tomb, and apostles who didn't believe it. Your line was not idle tales.

The same Sunday, in the afternoon. Two disciples are walking away from Jerusalem toward a village called Emmaus, about sixty furlongs off, seven miles or so. One is named Cleophas; the other Luke never names. They're going over everything that has happened, the way people do after a funeral. A stranger falls into step and asks what they're discussing. They stop, faces sad. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know? Luke tells this slowly, and the slowness is the point.
screen: `TWO WALKING AWAY.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `ARE YOU THE ONLY ONE WHO DOESN'T KNOW?`

segments.voice: They tell him the whole story, and their grief is in the past tense: we hoped that it was he that should have redeemed Israel. We hoped. The stranger walks them through the scriptures, beginning with Moses and all the prophets, showing what they said about the Christ. It takes miles. At the village, he makes as if to keep going, and they won't let him: "But they constrained him; saying: Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent. And he went in with them." At table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him: and he vanished out of their sight." Their hearts, they say, were burning while he opened the scriptures on the road, and that same hour they go back to Jerusalem to tell how he was known to them in the breaking of bread. Catholic teaching sees the shape of the Mass here. First the word: the scriptures opened and explained. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Saint John Paul the Second built his letter for the Year of the Eucharist around this scene and titled it with the disciples' plea in Latin, Mane nobiscum Domine, stay with us, Lord. And notice: he doesn't force his way in. He would have walked on. The invitation is theirs. Luke shows the risen Christ waiting to be asked.
screen: `WE HOPED.` · `THE SCRIPTURES OPENED ON THE ROAD.` · `STAY WITH US, IT IS TOWARDS EVENING.` · `KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.`

segments.voice: Think back over today as if it were a road: where were you walking, what were you talking about, what did you hope for that didn't happen? Let it be there, the way it was for those two, and picture the evening coming in. If you pray, use their words, stay with us, because it is towards evening; if you don't, just notice what you'd want to stay with you tonight.

Your line: stay with us. A plea at dusk, and a guest who said yes. Day four hundred eighty-eight, done.

489.title: Handle and see (Luke 24:36–43)
489.hook: he shows his hands and feet and eats a piece of broiled fish
489.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 24:35–48 on the Third Sunday of Easter in Year B of the Sunday cycle, and profess "the resurrection of the body" in the Apostles' Creed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emmaus: two travelers begged a stranger to stay, and knew him in the breaking of bread. Your line was stay with us.

A room in Jerusalem, that same Sunday evening. The two from Emmaus have just burst in, out of breath, telling how they knew him in the breaking of bread. Everyone is talking at once. And while they're still speaking, he is standing in the middle of them. Peace be to you. Nobody cheers. Luke says they were troubled and frightened, and thought they were seeing a spirit. A ghost. Jesus answers their fear plainly, with his hands and with a piece of fish.
screen: `THE EMMAUS TWO BURST IN.` → `HE STANDS IN THE MIDDLE.` → `THEY THINK IT'S A GHOST.`

segments.voice: He asks why they're troubled, and offers himself: "See my hands and feet, that it is I myself; handle, and see: for a spirit hath not flesh and bones, as you see me to have." Handle, and see. The Greek verb means to feel with the hands, the way you'd feel for a light switch in the dark. And still, Luke says, they didn't believe, for joy. Too happy to believe it. So he asks a very ordinary question: have you anything here to eat? "And they offered him a piece of a broiled fish, and a honeycomb." He took it and ate it in front of them. A ghost doesn't eat fish. It's a kitchen-table argument. Luke cares about bodies all the way through: a baby in a manger, a woman bent double, a servant's ear. He won't let the resurrection drift into a feeling or a memory. The Catechism says the same in its own way: the risen Jesus is not a ghost; he invites touch and shares a meal, and his body is truly his own, the one that was crucified, though now in a new, glorified state. That's why Catholics say in the Creed that they believe in the resurrection of the body. Not escaping the body. The body, raised.
screen: `TROUBLED: IT MUST BE A SPIRIT.` · `HANDLE, AND SEE.` · `THEY DISBELIEVED FOR JOY.` · `A PIECE OF BROILED FISH.` · then, large: `THE RESURRECTION OF THE BODY.`

segments.voice: If something small is nearby, a bite of bread, a piece of fruit, a glass of water, take it slowly and notice the weight in your hand, the taste, the swallow; if not, just picture your next meal. This body is alive, and it gets hungry, and that's not beneath faith. If you pray, give thanks for being alive in a body; if you don't, let the plain fact of eating be enough.
Broiled fish. What the risen Jesus ate in front of his frightened friends, proof that a spirit hath not flesh and bones. Today's word.
Your line: a ghost doesn't eat fish. The risen body, at a kitchen table. Until tomorrow.

A body, but they never saw it; they only heard his voice through the door.
A body, but only Peter was allowed to touch it; the others just watched.

490.title: He opened their understanding (Luke 24:44–49)
490.hook: the whole of the scriptures is about him
490.howItsDone: Catholics hear the scriptures at Mass in a pattern that pairs an Old Testament reading with the Gospel, and the Church teaches, in Dei Verbum, that the two Testaments are read in the light of each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday, broiled fish: in a frightened room, handle and see. Your line was a ghost doesn't eat fish.

Some books only make sense on the second read. The detective novel whose last chapter sends you back to page one, and suddenly every small detail was a clue. The film you rewatch knowing the twist. The disciples have had the scriptures all their lives: Moses, the prophets, the psalms, read aloud every Sabbath since they were children. They know the words. But tonight, still in that room, with the fish bones on the table, the risen Jesus gives them the last chapter, and sends them back to page one.
screen: `SOME BOOKS NEED A SECOND READ.` → `THEY KNOW THE WORDS ALREADY.` → `NOW, THE LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: He reminds them of what he told them while he was still with them: everything written about him in the law of Moses, in the prophets, and in the psalms had to be fulfilled. Those are the three parts of the scriptures as people in his time often named them: the whole book. Then the sentence that gives today its name: "Then he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures." Opened. It's the same Greek verb Luke has used all chapter. On the road, the scriptures were opened to the two from Emmaus. At the table, their eyes were opened. Now, minds. Reading the Bible well isn't only a matter of effort. Something has to be opened, and the risen Christ is the one who opens it. He sums it up: the Christ should suffer and rise again the third day, and repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning at Jerusalem. You are witnesses. Then: stay in the city until you are clothed with power from on high, a promise Luke keeps in his second book, Acts, at Pentecost. The Catholic Church still reads the scriptures this way. The Second Vatican Council, in Dei Verbum, says the two Testaments belong together, and quotes an old line from Saint Augustine: the New is hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New. Catholics also say the Old Testament keeps its own lasting worth, and the Jewish people read these same books in their own living tradition. Both are true at once.
screen: `MOSES, THE PROPHETS, THE PSALMS.` · `HE OPENED THEIR UNDERSTANDING.` · `ROAD, EYES, NOW MINDS.` · `THE NEW HIDDEN IN THE OLD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a line of scripture that has puzzled you, bothered you, or just slid past, maybe one from this week: green wood and dry, forgive them, the idle tales. Turn it over slowly without trying to solve it. If you pray, ask simply to understand it; if you don't, stay curious with it, the way you'd sit with a hard question from a friend.
He opened their understanding. The risen Jesus showing his disciples that the law, the prophets and the psalms speak of him. Today's word.
Your line: opened. And that's week seventy: green wood, Father, the centurion, idle tales, Emmaus, broiled fish, and opened.
screen: `WEEK SEVENTY: GREEN WOOD · FATHER · CENTURION · IDLE TALES · EMMAUS · BROILED FISH · OPENED`

fork.setup: you're the risen Christ with your friends for one evening. they've touched you and watched you eat. what do you give them next?
options: a new book to replace the old one.
a way to read the scriptures they already have.
a list of rules for the new community.
fork.reveal: he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures, the law, the prophets and the psalms, as speaking of him.

original.note: Greek: he opened up, the verb Luke uses for the scriptures, the eyes and the mind in chapter 24.

trapdoor: what you thought: the disciples finally studied hard enough.
what it means: the risen Christ opens their minds so the whole of the scriptures reads differently.
what a scholar hears: dianoigō runs through Luke 24 (vv. 31, 32, 45); law, prophets and psalms is an early way of naming the three parts of the Hebrew scriptures.

chat.says: What did Jesus mean that the law, the prophets and the psalms were about him?
options: That the whole of the scriptures speaks of him; he opened their minds to read it so.
That only the psalms really mention him; the law and prophets were about Israel.
That he had added new chapters to those books while he was teaching in Galilee.
chat.meaning: He opened their understanding to the law, the prophets and the psalms: the whole book. The Church says the two Testaments belong together.

Dei Verbum.meaning: Vatican II's teaching on Scripture; Latin: Word of God

Pentecost.meaning: when the Spirit came on the disciples, told in Acts

Saint Augustine.meaning: bishop and writer: the New is hidden in the Old

Second Vatican Council.meaning: a worldwide council of the Church in the 1960s
